cards.claim: Adapting polynomial coefficients at each iteration (Polar Express) converges faster than using fixed coefficients (Newton-Schulz), achieving the same accuracy with fewer iterations
cards.conditions: Synthetic matrices with singular values from 10^-3 to 10^3; degree-5 polynomial; comparing methods at same computational cost per iteration
cards.effect: ~2x faster convergence to a given error threshold; achieves good accuracy (error <1e-2) in 11 iterations vs 17+ for Newton-Schulz
cards.evidence: Numerical experiments comparing spectral norm error across iterations
cards.quote: When Polar Express is instantiated with , it dominates the other methods at every iteration, achieving excellent accuracy after just 11 iterations and converging about twice as fast as Newton-Schulz to any given error.

cards.claim: Adapting polynomial coefficients improves validation loss when training neural networks, with no wall-clock time penalty because computational cost per iteration is identical
cards.conditions: GPT-2-Small (124M) and GPT-2-Large (774M) training on 1B tokens from FineWeb dataset; bfloat16 precision; 5 iterations of degree-5 polynomial; Muon optimizer with AdamW on excluded parameters
cards.effect: Consistent validation loss improvement across all learning rates (e.g., GPT-Large: Polar Express 2.846 vs Jordan 2.885 vs You 2.873); equivalent training steps implies equivalent wall-clock time due to identical per-iteration cost
cards.evidence: Training GPT-2 models; validation loss curves across learning rates and epochs; comparison of training loss (nearly identical improvements) and wall-clock time
cards.quote: In both cases, muon-PolarExp achieves a better validation loss than muon-Jordan or muon-You. The advantage is remarkably consistent across all learning rates and epochs. Furthermore, since all three of these matrix sign methods are equally expensive (they all apply a degree 5 polynomial at each iteration), improved validation loss in terms of training steps also implies improved loss in terms of wall clock time.

cards.claim: The mechanism by which adaptive polynomials improve convergence: fixed Newton-Schulz suffers from inherently slow initial convergence, which adaptive methods address
cards.conditions: Polynomial approximation to matrix sign function; rectangular matrices; any degree ≥3
cards.effect: Adaptive methods achieve faster initial convergence while retaining asymptotic super-exponential convergence, eliminating the slow-start plateau of fixed methods
cards.evidence: Convergence analysis and comparison of methods; theoretical discussion of polynomial approximation properties
cards.quote: Due to the slow initial convergence of Newton-Schulz, Chen and Chow (2014) developed a version of the Newton-Schulz iteration, which adapts the polynomial at each iteration. The resulting method achieves a faster initial convergence, while retaining super-exponential convergence in later iterations.

cards.claim: Polar Express's adaptive polynomial selection is provably optimal: the greedy choice of polynomials per iteration minimizes worst-case error in the spectral norm
cards.conditions: Any degree d odd polynomial; any number of iterations k; singular values bounded by l_0 and u_0
cards.effect: Optimal worst-case approximation to matrix sign function; guaranteed convergence at least as fast as Newton-Schulz, strictly faster when degree ≥ 3
cards.evidence: Theorem 3.1 (optimality via equioscillation), Theorem 3.3 (convergence rates: quadratic for d=3, cubic for d≥5)
cards.quote: Our method constructs polynomials so that the resulting composition is the optimal approximation to the sign function with respect to the supremum ( ) norm ( Theorem 3.1 ). By iteratively applying these polynomials to , Polar Express computes an approximation to that is optimal in the worst-case.

cards.claim: Adapting polynomials provides faster convergence in early iterations (critical for low-precision deep learning) while maintaining asymptotic convergence guarantees
cards.conditions: bfloat16 precision; deep learning applications requiring GPU efficiency; low accuracy sufficient (worse than 16 digits acceptable)
cards.effect: Reaches usable accuracy within 5–10 iterations; converges roughly 2x faster than Newton-Schulz; practical for bfloat16 without significant precision loss
cards.evidence: Section 3.4 (finite precision handling); Figure 3 convergence curves; GPT-2 training experiments using 5 iterations
cards.quote: Polar Express computes an approximation to that is optimal in the worst-case... This early-stage acceleration is especially valuable in deep learning applications, where runtime efficiency takes precedence over high accuracy. In contrast, classical methods like Newton-Schulz suffer from a slow initial convergence.
